title.rendered: Coal plant proposals remain limited, but persistent across Africa

content.rendered:
Activity to develop coal-fired power plants in Africa was concentrated in a small number of countries. Less than 1GW of new coal capacity entered into operation in 2025:

  • 0.8GW in South Africa, and
  • 01.GW in Zimbabwe.

About 2GW of proposed coal plants were presumed shelved or cancelled in 2025 due to a lack of activity over multiple years.

The roughly 600 million Africans lacking access to electricity are creating strong incentives to rapidly deploy generation assets. This is increasingly being addressed through renewable energy and decentralised systems such as solar and mini-grids. This is reducing the need for large, new baseload thermal plants that use coal.

Other than in South Africa, coal-fired plants have never really taken off on the continent because persistent high financing cost—created by elevated risk premiums and limited access to affordable capity—remain a barrier to deployment.

“Many proposed projects have failed to advance over the past decade, with roughly 75% of proposals ultimately cancelled or shelved. Among the projects that have proceeded, many have done so through strong government backing or foreign investment,” according to the Global Energy Monitor’s 11th annual report into the way the world uses coal for power, Boom and Bust Coal 2026.

South Africa’s struggle with cost overruns and massive delays at the recently finished Kusile and Medupi power stations reinforces concerns about the financial risk associated with large coal developments in the region.

“As a result, Africa’s coal development pipeline has remained relatively stable around 14GW to 16GW since 2021, with new proposals often replacing older projects that fall away rather than driving sustained expansion.”

Zimbabwe and Zambia, coal twins

The GEM report shows that Zambia and Zimbabwe dominated new coal proposals in Africa in 2025. This is tied to the countries’ coal-based industrial development and efforts to get around declining hydropower generation driven by climate-induced droughts. The two countries account for 2.1GW of 3.1Gw of newly announced coal capacity on the continent.

Zimbabwe announced:

  • 0.3GW Kwekwe Indarama power station proposed to power a gold mine,
  • 0.2GW Sunny Yi Feng thermal power station is proposed to power a ferrochrome operation, and
  • GW Union Peak and 0.6GW Kalungwizi for grid-connected generation

To bring its coal fleet up to 1.8GW.

In 2025, Zambia proposed the development of:

  • The 0.3GW Amsons-Exergy thermal power station,
  • the 0.1GW Ezra Energy power station, and
  • two 67.5MW units at the Kazungula thermal power station.

Coal plant development across Africa is concentrated in just a few countries. While coal power is considered for industrial expansion and to deal with ongoing energy access and reliability challenges, declining renewable energy costs and the flexibility of decentralised energy systems are playing an increasingly important role in meeting Africa’s growing electricity demand.

Have you read? Coal usage for power taking on new dynamics

New coal plant proposals

New proposals on the rest of the continent remain sporadic:

  • Botswana announced plans for the 0.6GW New Morupule power station. This is even as the Morupule B coal plant continues to face significant problems and frequent outages. (It began operating in 2014);
  • Niger renewed its proposal for the 0.4GW second phase of the Salkadamna power station. This was first announced more than ten years ago, and both projects are still in the early stages of development.
  • Tanzania has periodically advanced plans to develop coal-fired power based on domestic coal reserves in the Ruhuhu Basin. These plans include projects at Mchuchuma and Kiwira. The country has two projects totalling 1.2GW on the cards as of 2025 but no capacity under construction. At one point, they had proposed building almost 2GW of coal power capacity. But these have been mostly delayed or cancelled.

Global Energy Monitor (GEM) notes that, historically, many coal plant proposals in West Africa have struggled to advance. This is due to financing constraints, uncertainty in the power market, and growing competition from renewable energy.

Across East Africa, some countries have proposed developing domestic coal reserves. This is in order to build their first coal plants, but few of these projects have moved forward.  

In Tanzania, the gap between ambition and implementation reflects “persistent barriers across the region, even as electricity access remains a pressing challenge — barriers that could potentially be overcome by smaller, more distributed renewable power with lower upfront costs and risk”, says GEM.

From the archives Phasing out coal projects in sub-Saharan Africa comes down to a matter of financing

Communities and coal

In Kenya, a decade of community opposition to the Lamu Power Project culminated in a 2025 ruling by the Environment and Land Court upholding a 2019 decision to revoke the project’s Environmental Impact Assessment approval.

Project owners Amu Power had revived their appeal of the revocation decision in 2024. But this was dismissed after the court found that the initial EIA process “had failed to include meaningful public participation by affected communities”.

Following President Xi’s 2021 decision that China should stop building new coal plants abroad, Asian countries have mostly halted financing stand-alone coal plants overseas. But it continues to propose coal projects for industrial facilities and offer private investment channels. Point in case would be two 2025 industrial proposals in Zimbabwe and the Kazungula proposal for Zambia.

Find out more in GEM’s Boom or Bust Coal 2026 report.

title.rendered: Rewiring reform: Is the great continental grid divide for everyone?

content.rendered:
Africa’s electricity sector struggles under fiscally weak utilities and ageing infrastructure. Unbundling and private participation are touted as key to improving finances, expanding access and powering the continent’s growth. But not everyone is buying what the World Bank is selling.

Africa sits at the bottom of the list for electricity generation capacity, per capita electricity consumption and household access to electricity. Power shortages are widespread, not least because power infrastructure is in disrepair and utilities are cash-strapped.

The changing demographics of the continent point to greater urbanisation over the next two decades, which will only put more pressure on governments to address the growing demand for water and electricity access.

The two determining factors for whether Africa’s electricity sector will be able to meet demand and expand access are:

  • financial sustainability of utilities, and
  • the ability of households to afford tariffs.

About two out of every five people in Africa still lack access to electricity (according to the IEA’s Financing Electricity Access in Africa report), and high costs often keep electricity out of reach for low-income households, who remain trapped in a poverty cycle they cannot escape.

Finance and investment remain significant barriers to addressing any of these problems.

excerpt.rendered: While unbundling and private participation are held up as a the way to power Africa’s growth, not all countries are liking this idea.

title.rendered: AI, energy affordability and water security

content.rendered:
Day One at Enlit Africa 2026 saw conference delegates explore how AI-enhanced weather forecasting can improve solar power dispatch planning and help transmission operators identify faults faster while reducing false alarms.

South Africa’s Department of Electricity and Energy Deputy Director General, Thabo Kekana, highlighted the country’s milestone of 365 days without loadshedding.

The conversation also turned to long-term energy security through grid expansion, storage, new generation capacity and affordable supply. In the water sector, Western Cape Province Head of Department of Water and Sanitation Zanele Bila-Mupariwa shared that water use licence authorisation timelines have been reduced from 300 days to 90 days.

Watch ESI Africa Editor-In-Chief Nicolette Pombo-van Zyl explains that affordability remains a major challenge for both electricity and water sectors across Africa and globally in this wrap up of Enlit Africa day one.

title.rendered: Using private sector to expand Africa’s transmission grid

content.rendered:
Increased private participation is gathering momentum in Africa as Kenya builds a dedicated transmission company, South Africa is prequalifying seven preferred businesses in its independent power transmission IPT programme and Uganda embarks on the early stages of its IPT programme.

Enlit Africa returns to the CTICC from 11 to 13 May in 2027

This was a sentiment that came out of a panel at Enlit Africa 2026 convened to discuss pertinent issues around the establishment of IPTs on the continent, made up of MD and CEO of the Kenya Electricity Transmission Company Kipkemoi Kibias, Nicholas Msibi Divisional CEO of ACTOM, and Project Manager at the Ministry of Energy in Uganda, Robert Mubiru [virtual].

The latter said because they are typically well integrated, national electricity utilities are better placed for the responsibility of creating the right operational environment. However there needs to come a time when open access is encouraged and the generation space opened up to allow more Independent Power Producers (IPPs) to participate.

“With industry electricity demand always evolving, driven by increased demand from sectors such as manufacturing and mining, electricity generation growth and transmission expansion is required. In Africa mining is a major economic activity, especially with expanding and new mines,” said Mubiru.

Have you read? AI and data centres can boost SA’s capability for renewable projects

He said without policies and regulations enabling private participation, particularly in transmission, it also becomes very difficult to achieve adequate generation and distribution. “The enabler is actually the integrated resource plan, where you review your power system particularly by looking at generation.

”Initially you need to look at the demand in terms of the growth projections, as well as the generation that you require to meet that demand, and then making a plan to transmit this power.”

Mubiru said that while there has traditionally not been a deliberate move by governments to try and allocate transmission lines to allow for private participation, this has started changing. “We’ve seen movements in the policies and regulations, and we hope that can be implemented in earnest so that more private participation is enabled.”

Bankable demand is desirable

Msibi said, while the capacity in terms of engineering to do this type of work, as well as the capacity to execute projects, is there the challenge is that the demand is not fixed. “It takes a lot of money to build a factories and upskill people, so if there is no demand then that leads to challenges.”

Kibias added that proper policy and laws on public-private partnerships (PPPs) are necessary to enable their quick implementation, even as they need time to be drafted. “After a slow start, we have been able to accelerate our progress in Kenya. And this has come after a very long process that required a lot of legal and policy drafting as well as support from institutions such as the World Bank to assist especially with human resource training.

“Which is why, after a slow process that started in 2018, in 2024 we were able to successfully sign our first project agreement after we had enacted our PPP policy and laws.”

content.rendered:
To gain greater insight into how the infrastructure investment sector is shaping up in in Africa, we spoke to Hans-Arild Bredesen, CEO of Bredesen Consulting and Enlit Africa advisory board member.

A key partner in the development of the Southern African Power Pool, he is currently assisting in the market design, market rules, and the development of the new trading platform for the Eastern African Power Pool. He see access to interconnected electricity grids as the next frontier for infrastructure investment on the continent.

What is attracting investment into Africa’s energy sector?

There is a lot of activity, and we see new investments being made in many southern and eastern African countries. The main bottleneck now is transmission access… within the country, but also between countries. These interconnections would enable more regional trade.

I think focusing on transmission will be a key enabler to maintain the investment pace in both Southern and Eastern Africa.

title.rendered: The importance of project feasibility to interconnected electricity projects

content.rendered:
To understand how interconnected electricity projects are put together, we spoke to Jacques Moulot, CEO and co-founder of the African Group for Energy, Water and Environment (A3E).

The role, and strength, of national utilities is not to be underestimated when creating multinational, regional interconnected electricity projects as the bankability of projects rests on the entity that will collect the payments, he explains.

What has shifted over the last decade about how projects in Africa are planned, developed and financed?

The shift has been slow. I would say there is more emphasis on energy equity, access and sustainability.

It is very clear that there are many different levels of planning. Some is done at national level, and others immediately at regional level. When it comes to large interconnections, they’re done at multi-country level, most of the time. When it’s for generation, it’s usually national, but it also needs to be connected outside the border to make those projects creditworthy and financeable.

So, I would say planning has evolved. There is now a greater emphasis on integrated resource energy planning, highlighting how projects can help countries achieve energy security in a more sustainable manner and ensure that the energy produced can be bought.

We are looking at the creditworthiness of the utilities, the market itself, and so forth. The players come together much earlier than in the past, and it’s a bit more systems-led than project-led.

title.rendered: Energy storage for grid flexibility in the long-term

content.rendered:
To get the inside story on Long Duration Energy Storage (LDES), we spoke with Oghosa Erhahon, the Policy and Markets Manager at the LDES Council, an organisation uniting global stakeholders under a shared mission to scale the technology.

LDES ultimately helps create a reliable, renewable grid by decoupling energy generation from consumption and addressing the intermittency of renewable energy sources, Erhahon explains.

What does Africa’s power system need as variable renewables increase and continue to scale?

One of the things we’ve seen in recent news is a significant increase in the amount of deployable renewable energy. In 2025, Africa recorded the fastest year for solar growth, with a remarkable 54% increase in installations alone. We expect to see a similar trajectory in wind capacity as well.

But beyond renewables and deployment, there’s the aspect to look into ‘what this means for grid stability’. So, this means assets and issues such as flexibility, erasure, frequency stability, and grid resilience. While we increase our renewables, we also need to figure out how our grids and energy systems will respond to the increase.

In practical terms, this means being able to respond quickly when supply and demand shift, maintaining system strengths, and ensuring renewable power doesn’t affect our power grid systems through changes in weather variability or climate-driven disruptions.

title.rendered: Compound your impact to shape real progress at Enlit Africa

content.rendered:
Enlit Africa exists to help you move the continent’s energy and water conversation from narrative to delivery, says Chanelle Hingston, Group Director: Power, Energy and Water, VUKA Group.

Africa does not need more words; we need action. We need to create properly prepared projects, establish partnerships focused on outcomes and not ambitions, and above all, build the infrastructure, not just plan the dreams.

This year’s Enlit Africa programme is built around a practical idea: compounding impact. Small shifts, made consistently, can create outsized outcomes over time. You will see that philosophy across the show as hard conversations are had on transmission and grid performance, investment conditions that unlock capital, municipal realities that determine whether reforms land, and the need for circularity in water resilience – all challenging environments that underpin economic continuity.

Enlit Africa is not designed to be a passive experience. You will get the most value out of your trip if you arrive with a plan. Plot out what sessions you want to attend, who you want to meet and what outcomes you hope to achieve. The show brings together utilities, government, municipalities, investors, developers and technology providers. That mix is intentional. We are creating the conditions for you to make real progress. title.rendered: Making the case for energy sovereignty in Africa

content.rendered:
With shocks becoming more frequent, from COVID-19 to Ukraine to the current US-initiated energy crisis, resilience in Africa is no longer about managing isolated disruptions. It is about constant adjustment and reform. African states have introduced emergency conservation and consumer support measures to shield citizens from fossil fuel price volatility. Yet long queues continue to form at fuel stations.

These interventions divert resources from essential programmes such as health and development. They may ease pressure in the short term, but they do not address the underlying problem. When energy supply remains inadequate and externally dependent, the continent is left in a state of subsidised vulnerability, exposed to global markets it cannot control.

Add ESI Africa as a preferred source on Google to your favourites for energy content you can trust

When power failures become health emergencies

When a clinic’s generator fails, the cost is not only operational. It is human. Health resilience is often measured through access and responsiveness, but it depends on a reliable electricity supply.

Across Africa, 50%-60% of health facilities lack reliable electricity. Cold chains for vaccines and oxygen supplies rely on expensive imported diesel. When fuel costs rise or supply chains tighten, facilities pass these costs on to patients. This becomes an additional burden at a moment of vulnerability.

In Nigeria, erratic price volatility can raise facility operating costs by up to 40% [according to Association of Nigerian Private Medical Practitioners] and increase out-of-pocket medical expenses by up to 20%.

In 2019, 95 million people in Africa faced catastrophic healthcare expenses. Energy insecurity turns treatable illness into financial crisis. Health resilience depends on energy sovereignty. Health systems cannot function reliably when they depend on volatile global fuel markets.

Of interest to you Burundi inaugurates first solar-powered health facilities as national expansion advances

Industrialisation needs reliable power

Adaptive capacity requires more than endurance. It requires the ability to shift structurally. Informal work remains a central survival strategy to livelihoods across Africa, accounting for 83& of employment. Its productivity is limited, often constrained by unreliable energy access.

Moving workers into stable employment requires industrialisation. Industrialisation depends on consistent and secure power. Factories cannot operate on intermittent supply or fuel imports that become scarce when external conditions change.

When energy systems are unstable or externally controlled, they impose limits on industrial growth. This restricts value-added manufacturing and keeps young people in precarious work. Energy sovereignty provides the foundation for sustained industrial activity and long-term employment.

Of reference Geopolitical, economic risks rise in new age of global competition

The cost of importing energy vs energy sovereignty in Africa

Energy dependency also acts as a financial drain on both states and households. Reliance on dollar-denominated fuel imports exports capital in exchange for short-term stability. This weakens the ability to build domestic savings and invest in infrastructure. At household level, high energy costs reduce disposable income and limit investment in education or productive assets.

Expanding domestic energy production, particularly from renewable sources, can reduce this outflow. It allows countries to retain capital and reinvest it locally. Energy sovereignty strengthens national balance sheets and supports long-term economic development.

At the recent Power Africa Summit [held in Washington DC in March 2026], it was stated that the goal of energy is to expand human opportunity. Current geopolitical tensions show how fragile externally dependent systems can be. Africa has abundant renewable resources. Solar, wind, and hydropower offer a path to greater stability.

Developing these resources can reduce exposure to global price shocks and strengthen domestic control. Resilience depends on the ability to maintain energy supply on reliable terms.

About the author
Nyasha Munodawafa is a Policy Researcher and Financial Economist at Enzi Ijayo, a Pan African think and do tank that convenes academia, private sector, civil society and governments to analyse and formulate policies for growing investments in green energy solutions that provide a sustainable path towards greening Africa’s economic development

title.rendered: Policies driving clean cooking access across Africa

content.rendered:
Following slow progress on energy access between 2020 and 2024, policy momentum on clean cooking and electricity access is starting to build again, particularly in Africa.

Governments are reinvigorating domestic efforts, with 56 new electricity access policies being implemented or announced since the 2024 IEA Summit on Clean Cooking in Africa, alongside 64 new clean cooking initiatives. Sub-Saharan Africa accounts for the majority of this renewed activity.

Still, disruptions stemming from the conflict in the Middle East threaten progress, especially in clean cooking. LPG import prices increased by an average of 80% in March 2026 in developing economies (where it is widely is used for clean cooking) following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

According to the IEA’s State of Energy Policy 2026 report, this increase has prompted many governments to take steps “to stabilise prices, often straining public finances or the finances of local energy companies”.

“Some countries have implemented emergency demand-restraint measures, increased domestic production, rationed non-essential uses of liquefied petroleum gas and encouraged fuel switching where possible.”

Have you read? Policy development meant to strengthen global energy access insufficient to meet SDG7

Effects of geopolitics

The IEA’s report suggests that supply disruptions and price increases have had immediate effects on energy use, “with an estimated one out of six households expected to shift from LPG back to traditional use of biomass for cooking”.

Some countries are

  • implementing emergency demand restraint measures,
  • increasing domestic production where feasible,
  • prioritising supply to households, hospitals and schools,
  • rationing commercial use of LPG, and
  • encouraging fuel switching where possible.

The IEA-hosted Summit on Clean Cooking in Africa played a significant role in raising political commitment and fostering partnerships among decision makers to tackle this challenge.

Building on this momentum, the G20 endorsed the Clean Cooking Infrastructure Investment and Action Plan—an outcome of South Africa’s G20 Presidency—which lays out concrete steps countries can take to advance progress on clean cooking.

The G7 also reiterated its commitment to supporting access to clean cooking as part of its Call to Action on Enhancing Energy Security.

Listen to find out more: Clean cooking and critical minerals discussions at G20

Clean cooking in Africa

Progress on new clean cooking policy initiatives has been strongest in Africa, where three-quarters of people without clean cooking access live in countries that recorded positive policy progress in 2025.

Many countries also updated or introduced new clean cooking targets in 2025. “As a result, more than 70% of the global population without access to clean cooking now live in countries with a clean cooking target.”

Since early 2024, more than 50 clean cooking policies, including 17 new national targets, have been adopted. Countries such as Ghana, Kenya, Malawi, Mozambique, Nigeria, Tanzania, Uganda and Zimbabwe now show the broadest coverage across key clean cooking policy areas.

  • Tanzania’s National Clean Cooking Strategy (2024-34) targets 80% access by 2034 through measures to “raise public awareness and enhance the accessibility and affordability of clean fuels and appliances while promoting investment and harmonising existing policies”.
  • Ethiopia launched its National Clean Cooking Roadmap in 2025 to support its ambition to meet universal access to clean cooking.
  • Nigeria’s Federal Executive Council approved the National Clean Cooking Policy in March 2024. This includes measures to create a sustainable local clean cooking industry and boost access.

What next?

Rapid expansion of clean cooking solutions can be achieved by developing new strategies and targets and strengthening existing ones using clear and detailed implementation plans and funding mechanisms.

Tax measures which are used to reduce the cost of clean cooking equipment and fuels for consumers also feature in recently introduced policies. Since 2024, seven countries have changed their VAT rules or tariffs on clean cooking equipment or fuels.

  • Kenya reduced its VAT on denatured bioethanol to zero in 2025.
  • Nigeria’s National Clean Cooking Policy exempts liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) and biogas, along with related equipment such as conversion kits, biogas digesters, compressors and clean cooking accessories from VAT.
  • Uganda removed VAT from biomass pellets, bioethanol and ethanol stove components, and
  • Tanzania has announced plans to lower taxes and levies on clean cooking appliances and energy-efficient stoves.
